1:
Whether the verse threatens or comforts is the whole question. Calvin reports the reading he does not take, that many understand the words as a threat of an affliction heavier than the two already suffered, the first under Tiglath-pileser and the second which carried the tribes away and blotted out the name of the nation. He grants the view does not want plausibility and still prefers the other, that the prophet begins to comfort the wretched by the hope of alleviation, so that they may not be swallowed up by the huge mass of their distresses; the chastisements now to be inflicted will be lighter than those before. He then raises the objection against himself, that this later calamity was to raze Jerusalem, throw down the temple and abolish the sacrifices, which the earlier ones had left untouched. Wesley takes the comforting sense without the argument: the calamity shall be great and yet not such as the king of Assyria brought, who at first dealt more gently but afterwards rooted them out.

Gill turns the verse the other way with two renderings, that there shall be no weariness to him that afflicts them, or no fleeing from him that is oppressed in it; on either the words amplify the distress rather than mitigate it, though he admits many interpreters take them as comfort, which is the sense of the received version. He also names the oppressor differently: where an older commentator understood the king of Assyria, Gill prefers Titus Vespasian, indefatigable in carrying on the siege of Jerusalem and in distressing the people in all quarters.

Ellicott holds the difficulty manufactured by the printers. It is obvious even in the English version, he says, that the chapters are wrongly divided and that what follows belongs to the same utterance as what precedes; and he calls that version so obscure as to be almost unintelligible, requiring an entire remodelling, which he supplies: there is no gloom to her that was afflicted, for in the former time he brought shame on the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter he bringeth honour on the way by the sea, beyond Jordan, the circuit of the Gentiles. On that reading the picture of extreme misery at the close of the previous chapter dissolves and another takes its place, the region laid waste becoming the scene of a glory greater than Israel had known. Clarke notes the same division from the other side, that this verse stands as the last verse of the preceding chapter in the Hebrew, and renders the first word as accumulated darkness.

Why these two tribes are named is answered much alike. Clarke identifies the country as Galilee round the sea of Gennesareth, the parts that principally suffered in the first Assyrian invasion, and the first to enjoy the blessings of the preaching of the Gospel. Wesley says these parts are mentioned because the storm fell most heavily upon them, but that under them the other parts of the land are understood; he explains the sea as the lake bordering the portions of Zebulun and Naphtali, and the name of the region as taken from its bordering upon the Gentiles. Henry takes the naming as a lesson in method: God tries what less judgments will do with a people before he brings greater, and if a light affliction does not humble and reform us we must expect to be afflicted more grievously. But his weight falls on the first word of the verse. In the worst of times, he says, the people of God have a nevertheless to comfort themselves with, something to allay and balance their troubles; and it is matter of comfort, when things are darkest, that he who forms the light and creates the darkness has appointed to both their bounds, and can say how far the dimness shall go and no further.
2:
Who is walking in the darkness is settled differently by each. Gill rejects the older identifications, Judah and Jerusalem under siege in the days of Hezekiah and the people in Egypt as one ancient paraphrase has it, and fixes on the inhabitants of Galilee in the times of Christ; he then makes it a character of all the people of God before conversion, shut up in unbelief and walking on without knowing whither they go. Keil and Delitzsch say the range of vision is extended, but not to the Gentiles, only to all Israel, and add that salvation would not break forth until it had become utterly dark along the whole horizon. Wesley takes the people for Israel and Judah together and the darkness as a general word covering calamity, ignorance, idolatry and profaneness. Ellicott hears the words throwing us back on the close of the previous chapter, where a light shines on forlorn and weary wanderers who had walked in the valley of the shadow of death.

How the verse is used in the Gospel divides them further. Ellicott grants the quotation and limits it: the words are quoted of the ministry in Galilee, but we cannot positively say such a fulfilment was in the thoughts of the prophet, since the context shows he was thinking of Assyrian invasions and of a nation growing strong in numbers; the Evangelist adapts the words to a further meaning than was apparently in the mind of the writer, and interprets them by his own experience. Calvin admits the difficulty and settles it the other way. Matthew, he says, appears to torture the passage to a different meaning, yet on a just view of the comparison has applied it correctly; the commentators who merely assert that it belongs to the kingdom of Christ do not show how, whereas the prophet, speaking of the return from Babylon, does not look to a single age but includes all the rest until Christ came, that deliverance being only a prelude to the restoration of the Church.

The next verse turns on one small word, and the copies are divided. Clarke reports that eleven manuscripts of one collation and six of another, with two ancient versions, read increased their joy rather than not increased the joy. Ellicott prefers the same marginal reading, since the picture is one of unmingled brightness, a return as of a golden age with the population growing as never before, which scarcely admits the shadow the text introduces, unless we see with some critics a contrast between an outward prosperity that held no permanent joy and the abundance of joy under the ideal king. Keil and Delitzsch, keeping the negative, find one intelligible sense for it, that the nation is one to which God had formerly not given great joy, which must mean by understatement the nation he had plunged into deep sorrow; and they call even that unnatural. Calvin canvasses more solutions than anyone and takes none: the reading that turns the particle into a pronoun, the proposal to make the first clause a question, the application to the army of Sennacherib which brought its king no joy, the application to the Church because believers are subject to afflictions, and the application to the calling of the Gentiles. He reads it instead as a repetition of the comparison he began the chapter with, that this blessing of redemption is greater than all others, though it might seem unworthy of such praise on account of the small number redeemed.

On the joy itself Ellicott makes much of the words before thee: the gladness is that of worshippers at a sacrificial feast, the harvest being its peaceful side and the dividing of spoil the rejoicing after conflict. Wesley reads the multiplying as the promise to Abraham about his seed, made good by the gathering in of the Gentiles.
4:
The yoke is read at two levels. Wesley keeps it literal: the burdensome yoke, the staff by which the man was forced to carry burdens, the rod wherewith he was beaten, and the oppressor, which he extends to all oppressors but especially to sin and the devil. Gill takes the verse spiritually and names three deliverances, from the yoke of the ceremonial law, from the tyranny of Satan, and from the dominion of sin. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew brings the yoke forward with all the emphasis of position, and hears a bondage like that of Egypt, where the taskmasters, named by the same word rendered oppressor here, drove the people to their labours with rods. Keil and Delitzsch hear the same echo and draw a consequence: this deliverance would be the counterpart of the Egyptian, except that the whole nation was redeemed then whereas only a small remnant would share the final redemption, which is why the prophet reaches instead for the day of Midian, when Gideon broke a seven years dominion not with an army but with a handful of resolute warriors. Ellicott suggests the allusion was prompted by the division of spoil already in the mind of the prophet, since of all victories in the history of Israel that one was most conspicuous for plunder; men remembered it centuries after, as we remember Poitiers and Agincourt.

The next verse turns on a word found nowhere else. Clarke reports that one lexicographer fairly tells us we may guess its meaning from the context, and that Jewish interpreters explain it as battle or conflict, which he believes is guesswork too; but something seems rather to be meant that could burn along with the garments named beside it. Since in Syriac the word means a shoe, he takes it for the armour covering the legs and feet, and renders the phrase the greaves of the armed warrior. Ellicott re-translates the whole verse to the same effect, that every boot of the warrior that tramps noisily, and the cloak rolled in blood, shall be for burning, as fuel for fire; the victory is decisive and the weapons of war are burnt up. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by elimination, since the closing statement requires the sense of a combustible thing, which shuts out the renderings noise and din; they allow that military equipment would be admissible, while noting that the change of letters it depends on cannot be established from the dialects.

Those keeping the received rendering make the noise the point. Gill fills it out with trumpet and drums, the shoutings of soldiers, the stamping of horses and the clashing of swords and shields. Wesley hears the exclamations of the conqueror and the lamentations of the conquered, and reads the contrast that follows as a victory more terrible to the adversaries, whom God will consume as it were by fire. Calvin states the contrast as the settled view: others conquer by making a great slaughter, but here the Lord will conquer by his own hand alone, and when he acts by himself every covering is removed and we perceive more clearly that he is the author of our salvation. On that ground he insists the connective in the middle of the verse be rendered adversatively, rejects the alternative that makes the second clause continue the first, and holds the subject to be not merely the deliverance that let the people return under Cyrus but the kingdom of Christ.

Clarke alone supports the burning from outside the text. Gathering armour from a battlefield and burning it as an offering to the god supposed to have given the victory was a heathen custom, and the Romans made the act an emblem of peace; he cites a medal struck by Vespasian showing the goddess Peace setting fire to a heap of armour, and a passage of Virgil on the same practice.
6:
The identity of the child is settled the same way by everyone, against the same alternative. Gill takes it of the Messiah, as an ancient paraphrase does, and refuses the application to Hezekiah on two grounds: he could never be represented as a child just born, being ten or eleven when the prophecy was given, and no reason can be assigned why he should be called a son in so unusual a manner. Wesley makes the same point from the history of interpretation, that the ancient Hebrew doctors and the Chaldee paraphrast understood the place of the Messiah, and that the titles cannot be ascribed to any mortal man. Calvin rejects the other application on chronology, since that king was born before the prediction was uttered, whereas the prophet speaks of something new and unexpected, meant to arouse believers to expect a future event. Keil and Delitzsch identify him with the child of the earlier prophecy: the son of the virgin who would come to maturity in troublous times is here already born and in possession of the government, appearing there as a sign and here as a gift of grace.

Why the verse stands where it does is answered two ways. Keil and Delitzsch see the prophet building on the two sentences before: the reason for the triumph is the deliverance, the reason for the deliverance the destruction of the foe, and the reason for all the joy the new great King. Calvin argues from the design of the passage, that this deliverance is preferable to the other benefits of God because he will not only bring the people back from captivity but set Christ on his throne, so that the kindness covers the whole period during which the Church was preserved. He sees no absurdity in the transition from the return of the ancient people to a restoration centuries later, since the return from Babylon began a renovation completed when Christ appeared; and the lesson is that they were rescued from death not only to live in the land of Canaan but to arrive at the kingdom of God.

Ellicott alone asks where the language came from. The picture of a kingdom of peace could not be complete without a king, and in describing him the prophet uses words which cannot find complete fulfilment in any child of man; yet there was a law of continuity, and the form of the prediction was developed from earlier writers, the king-priest of one psalm, the anointed King addressed as a son in another. The mysterious names the prophet had given his own children fed the same thought. The surrounding courts supplied its shape, since the kings of Egypt and Assyria delighted in long lists of epithets describing their greatness, so it was natural the prophet should give his own king a name formed after that fashion but full of a greater majesty.

On the titles the voices differ over how to count them. Ellicott holds that what follows is one name, not many, of eight words whose last six fall into three couplets. Wesley says the name is not a description of a name but of a glorious nature and its qualities, and explains the first title from the office: he has been the counsellor of his church in all ages and the author of the counsels delivered by prophets and apostles. Clarke works on them singly, rendering one as the prevailing or conquering God and another as the Father of the everlasting age, and noting that the Greek version gives instead the Messenger of the Great Counsel; what rests on the shoulder, he explains, is the ensign of government, the sceptre or sword or key, borne upon or hung from it. He also reports a reading he finds nowhere else, from a thirteenth-century manuscript, which inserts before the clause about the government that he shall be a stumbling-block.
7:
The verse opens with a scribal oddity that three voices stop for. Clarke reports that in the common Hebrew Bibles the first word is written with the closed or final form of a letter in the middle of it, though twelve manuscripts of one collation and twelve of another have the open form; the closed letter, he says, is supposed to contain mysteries, that Jerusalem shall be shut up and confined till the days of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch report another tradition attached to the same letter, that God had designed to make Hezekiah the Messiah and his invader the last enemy, and that because the king was not found worthy the letter was closed; they allow there is some sense in it, so far as Messianic hopes really could centre for a time on that king. Calvin notes the irregularity without a legend, observing only that the form which properly belongs to the end of a word is used here in the middle, and reaching for a comparison a reader would feel: a Greek scholar would have been startled at seeing the final form of a letter where the ordinary one belongs.

How a kingdom can be said both to be perpetual and to increase is the substance of the verse. Calvin makes the continuance twofold, belonging to time and to quality: though the kingdom of Christ appears at every moment about to perish, God not only defends it but extends its boundaries far and wide and carries it forward in uninterrupted progression. We must not judge its stability from the present appearance of things, he says, but from the promise; and since the mightiest of this world are suddenly overturned while this alone is unchangeable, the shocks by which the Church is shaken need not weaken faith. He ties the peace to the government as inseparable from it, so that those daily exposed to innumerable vexations may keep composure amid the destruction of the whole world. Gill measures the increase historically, as the spreading of the Gospel: at first preached only in Judea, then carried into the Gentile world with great success; he compares the growth to the stone cut out of the mountain without hands which filled the whole earth, and to the mustard seed, least of all seeds, which becomes a tree in which the birds of the air build their nests. Clarke states the same expansion flatly, that this prince has all power in heaven and earth, that his government is daily more and more extended, and that every act of it is regulated according to wisdom and goodness.

On the throne and the zeal the comment turns finer. Ellicott notes that the throne of David, though in harmony with the whole body of prophetic tradition about the Messiah, appears here for the first time in this prophet; and he weighs what the closing words promise. They admit, he says, of being interpreted of the perpetuity of a dynasty of which the anointed king is the founder, but the everlasting Father of the preceding verse and the parallels elsewhere favour a personal immortality of sovereignty instead. Wesley takes the same words for the promise made to David and to his seed, and reads the whole as extending to all the ends of the earth. On the last clause Ellicott observes that the same root serves in Hebrew, as in Greek, for zeal and for jealousy, and thinks the second idea dominant here: it is because God loves the daughter of Zion with an absorbing love that he purposes such great things for her future, and that what he purposes will assuredly be performed. Wesley reads the same clause as a guarantee of agency, that the work shall be brought to pass by almighty God out of the fervent affection he has to his own glory and to his people.
8:
Every voice marks a turn here. Gill has the prophet, having comforted Judah with the promise of the Messiah, return to denounce judgment on the ten tribes, and insists the word sent is not the comfortable word just spoken but a word of threatening, sent beforehand by the prophets to warn them, so that when it came to pass they would know their ruin was of the Lord and not a matter of chance. Wesley says the same in two lines: the prophet, having inserted some consolatory passages, returns to his former charge, and the past tense is the prophetical style, meaning the thing shall certainly be accomplished. Ellicott calls it a new section, still closely connected with the same historical occasion: the vision of the glory of the far-off king comes to an end and the prophet returns to the more immediate surroundings of his own time. Calvin agrees that a new prediction begins, and supplies the political setting, that the kingdom about to be described was then hostile to the Jews, who had good cause to fear its forces once it made a league with its neighbour.

Whose ruin is meant divides the voices sharply. Keil and Delitzsch set out the difficulty as two questions, whether the section is directed against the northern kingdom only or against all Israel, and what the standpoint of the prophet himself was. They report that most commentators answer the first by confining it to Ephraim, and hold that incorrect: the prophet commences with Ephraim but does not stop there, and the fates of the two kingdoms flow into one another as they were causally connected in fact. Nor can it be maintained that Ephraim had already felt the scourge when these words were uttered; the prophet stands at a time when judgment after judgment had fallen upon all Israel without improving it. Ellicott divides the names the other way. Whether the two stand in a parallelism of identity or of contrast is a question, and the usage of the earlier chapters makes identity more probable; on that reading both stand practically for the kingdom of Judah as the true representative of Israel, the apostate kingdom being no longer worthy of the name and described here simply as Ephraim. Calvin treats the two names as one and finds the doubling rhetorical: the diversity of expression is elegant, and shows that the wicked gain nothing when they try to turn the judgment of God aside or alter it. He hears behind it the speech of men who think to escape by their witticisms and turn all that the prophets threaten into jest, as if one were to drive away a storm by the breath of his mouth.

Henry reads the verse as a preface and draws the lesson out of the order of events. The threatenings are directed primarily against the ten tribes, whose ruin came within a few years, but they look further, to all the enemies of the throne and kingdom of Christ. God warns before he wounds: he sent notice by his prophets of what he would do, that they might meet him in the way of his judgments, and because they took no care to turn away his wrath it lighted upon them, for no word of God shall fall to the ground. Henry pictures it falling as a storm of rain and hail they could not avoid, and adds that those willingly ignorant of the wrath of God revealed against sin shall be made to know by feeling what they would not know by hearing. Keil and Delitzsch state the same sequence in one sentence, that the great light would not arise until the darkness had reached its deepest point. Clarke stays with the text, reporting that thirty manuscripts of one collation, many of another, and three printed editions read the divine name here in place of the title.
9:
The verb rendered shall know is left without an object, and each voice supplies one. Gill offers three: they shall know the word of the Lord and by sad experience feel its weight, or shall know the whole of it and find every particular accomplished, or shall be punished, since the same word is frequently used in that sense in Arabic. Wesley supplies the object from the quarrel itself, that they shall know whether the word be true or false. Calvin makes the knowing a matter of actual experience and hears a reproof of their unbelief: since the prophet speaks to the deaf, and they set no value on the warnings, the event itself will teach them, but too late. Clarke alone treats the gap as a fault in the text. The verb stands destitute of its object and the sense is imperfect, he says, and one ancient version alone reads otherwise, rendering it that they carry themselves haughtily; that version seems therefore to have read a different verb, which agrees well with what follows and clears up the difficulty. He reports two conjectures besides, one attaching the verb to the speech in the next verse and one making it that they are become wicked, and rejects the second as a mere confusion of two similar letters.

Who speaks is not in doubt. Calvin insists the people meant are not the Jews but the Israelites, the prophet naming them expressly and adding their capital; fortified cities, he observes, conceiving themselves beyond the reach of danger, are much more insolent in their pretensions, and think they will always have the remedy in their own hands by capitulating with the enemy, though the whole country were laid waste. Wesley names them as briefly, the proudest of the tribes and the strongest place, the seat of the king and court.

The boast itself is explained from the building trade. Clarke reports that eastern bricks are only clay moistened with water and mixed with straw and dried in the sun, so that such walls are no better than mud walls, properly opposed to hewn stone as greatly superior in beauty and durableness; the sycamore, whose grain is remarkably coarse and spongy, could stand in no competition with the cedar. By this figurative and sententious speech, he concludes, they boast that they will easily repair their losses and bring their affairs to a more flourishing condition than ever; and he adds that some of the bricks he describes lie before him, brought from the site of ancient Babylon, with the straw visible kneaded into the clay. Ellicott divides the same materials by class, sun-dried brick and cheap sycamore for the dwellings of the poor, hewn stone and cedar for the palaces of the rich, and warns that the words are too proverbially figurative for a literal interpretation; whatever injury the city had sustained, its rulers thought it only the prelude to a greater victory than any they had won. Gill takes the fallen brick for the houses outside the besieged cities, of which the haughty inhabitants made no account, reckoning such a desolation little or no loss. Wesley reduces the speech to a sentence: they have received some damage but do not doubt they will quickly repair it with advantage.

Calvin hears the settled temper of men who despised a calamity as if it had been of advantage, since it gave them occasion to adorn their houses and fields with greater splendour, and he refuses to leave it in the past. This was not the fault of a single age, he says: how many are the distresses with which Europe has been afflicted these thirty or forty years, and yet luxury increases every day and men go on in their crimes more shamelessly than ever, the very calamities having become excitements to splendour. What then should we expect but to be bruised with heavier blows.
11:
The threat is that an alliance is about to fail them. Gill explains that the adversaries are set up on high, exalted above him and made his conquerors, and identifies them as the Assyrians who took Damascus and slew the king of Syria; the name is mentioned because the Israelites put great trust in that prince, their ally, so that the threat abates the pride just expressed. Wesley says the same more briefly: it is to chastise their pride and defeat their hopes, the confederate being named because he was confederate with Ephraim, and the pronoun at the end referring not to him but to Ephraim. Calvin makes the reversal the point: a people proud of their alliance and hoping everything would succeed are threatened with a change that takes away all their hope, since the Assyrians afterwards took arms against the Syrians and that country was ruined; and he reads the joining of enemies as God gathering various nations and commissioning them, as the soldiers of that vast monarchy were themselves drawn from many. Ellicott notices that the Hebrew tenses are past, probably representing the vision as an accomplished future, and offers the historical solution that Syria, after its conquest, was compelled to join a campaign against Samaria; so the very nations whose support the northern kingdom had counted on are among the enemies joined against it.

Clarke works instead on the letters. For the word rendered enemies one scholar conjectured a similar word meaning princes, a reading Clarke finds confirmed by some thirty manuscripts and by nine more that carry an erasure at just that letter and so probably read princes at first; on that reading it is the princes of the late ally, the Syrians named in the next verse, who shall now be excited against Israel. He reports a second variation from the Greek version, which reads Mount Zion for the royal name, so that God would be setting up the adversaries of Mount Zion, the Syrians and the Philistines, against Israel.

Whether the two enemies are placed by the compass is the next question, and Calvin stands alone. Gill takes the Syrians as coming from the rising of the sun and the Philistines from its setting, since Syria lay east of the land and the other people west; Wesley agrees, and adds that though the king of Syria was destroyed the nation survived, submitted to the king of Assyria, and at his command invaded Israel afterwards, devouring like wild beasts. Calvin refuses the geography. He does not agree with those who make the words mean those on the east and those on the west; the more natural meaning is that the enemies will invade on every side, because on all sides those regarded as faithful friends will rise up to destroy them, the phrases agreeing with ordinary modes of speaking, so that we need not seek an interpretation new and foreign to the purpose. Clarke reaches the same sense from the other phrase, rendering the open mouth as on every side, in every corner of their country, pursuing them to the remotest extremities.

Calvin then draws his lesson, that we should learn what it is to rely on human power and the alliances of kings, and what it is to grow careless through being entangled in unlawful covenants; for as soon as the Lord pleases, those formerly on our side will in the smallest portion of time be turned against us, and the remedies we thought useful will prove our destruction. He adds that God does not expend all his scourges at once, but when we proceed obstinately increases and multiplies the chastisements. Ellicott hears the same law in the closing refrain, noting that a formula applied earlier to Judah is used here of Israel at large and especially of Ephraim, and that it embodied the rule which governed the dealing of God with both.
13:
The blows continue because they have done no work. Gill has the Lord smiting with the rod of correction to bring the people to a sense of their sin, and finds them returning neither by repentance nor, as an ancient paraphrase puts it, to his worship; afflictions, he says, unless sanctified, are of no use to restore backsliders. He notices that the prophet calls them simply the people, not my people nor the people of the Lord, because unworthy of the character, and reports two versions rendering it that they returned not until they were smitten, as though they did return then, which the context contradicts. Ellicott says only that there were no proofs of the conversion which true prophets and preachers have at all times sought. Calvin turns the clause into a scale of guilt. It is heinous when men do not receive instruction as soon as it is delivered, more heinous when rebukes do not affect them, most heinous when in spite of chastisements they grow hardened and inflame the indignation of the Judge; when no remedies produce any good effect, what must we think but that the disease is incurable. Where there is no repentance, he adds, it is unreasonable to expect God to yield to obstinate men as if vanquished; and the rebuke applies not to the Israelites only but to us.

The sentence that follows spares nobody, and on that they agree. Calvin reads it as universal vengeance involving all ranks, since the contagion had spread until no part was left sound; and he notices the self-excuse that abundant wickedness breeds, since when iniquity abounds every one flatters himself, thinking he is hidden under an admirable veil because so many are like him. Wesley reduces the pairs to high and low, the goodly branches of tall trees being the mighty and noble and the bulrush the weakest, and takes the day named as meaning all together, one as well as another. Ellicott presses the figures closer: the branch is strictly that of the palm, whose stately height answered to the nobles of the land, while the rush, emblem of a real or affected lowliness, represented the mean man. Clarke notes only that thirteen manuscripts read a different preposition in the phrase about the day, and that another shows an erasure at that letter.

The explanation of the figure raises its own question. Calvin observes that the prophet expounds only half of what he said allegorically, making the head the princes at the helm of the commonwealth and the tail the prophets, while saying nothing of the branch and the rush; the reason, he suggests, is that he meant to press hardest on the transgressors who led others into sin through the influence of their rank. He denies that the name of tail implies contempt, holding that it denotes the lowest parts of one body, and compares the one class to lions or bears and the other to foxes. Gill defines the first term as the elder in office rather than in age, honoured for dignity and riches, and reports two versions rendering it instead of those who have the persons of men in admiration, the character given elsewhere of false teachers. Wesley explains why the false prophets are named among the losses: not that it is a punishment to lose such persons, but partly to show the extent of the calamity and partly to beat down vain presumptions of peace, by showing that those who fed their hopes should perish with their prophecies. Ellicott alone reports that some critics reject the verse as a marginal note that crept into the text, and answers that the prophet may well have interpreted his own formula; to him, as to a later prophet, no class was so contemptible as spiritual guides whose policy was a time-serving selfishness, the corruption of the best being the worst of all.
16:
The charge against the leaders is that they did not lead. Wesley identifies them as the false prophets, working by false doctrines and evil counsels. Gill reports that several ancient versions render the word instead as those who bless the people. Calvin knows a rendering making the sense that nothing is more destructive to a nation than flatteries, which encourage unbounded licentiousness, but keeps his earlier reading and states the fault as neglect: rulers whose duty it was to restrain the people within the limits of decent behaviour let all indulge freely in crimes, and are justly reckoned corrupters, since corruption flows from them to the whole body as from the head to the members. Magistrates and pastors are appointed to restrain waywardness and defend the honour of God, and neglecting this they are impostors rather than guides, for when every one does as he pleases there can be nothing but the most terrible result. Yet Calvin will not let the led shelter behind them: bad rulers are no cloak for our own transgressions, since none are ruined by treacherous guides but those who of their own accord wish to be led astray.

That the judgment spares neither the young nor the bereaved strikes them next. Ellicott notes that the severity spares not even the flower of the youth of the nation, nor the widows and orphans who were the special objects of compassion to God and man, and that the refrain closing the verse tolls again like the knell of doom. Calvin makes the same point from custom, that boys and youths and widows are usually spared even amidst dreadful slaughter, as the heathen spared them at the sacking of towns, whereas here the Lord threatens to regard neither sex nor age. Lest anyone accuse God of cruelty he adds the reason: the word rendered hypocrite means an ungodly and treacherous man and points to the source of all the evils, that there was no true fear of God among them, not a slight dissimulation but an inward contempt by which consciences are stupefied. Ellicott renders the neighbouring word blasphemy or villainy. Wesley qualifies the universal terms, since every one is not to be taken precisely, seven thousand elect persons having been among them when they seemed to Elijah universally corrupt; the body of the people is meant, called hypocrites because though they professed to worship God they had forsaken him.

The fire at the end is read as both sin and punishment. Gill takes the burning wickedness for the punishment of their sins, or for the wicked consumed by divine vengeance, and says the sense is the same either way. Clarke has wickedness raging like a fire and laying waste the nation, but proving its own destruction by bringing down the fire of the wrath of God to burn the briers and thorns, the wicked themselves; the image, he notes, is frequently applied in Scripture to the rage of the wicked, violent yet impotent and of no long continuance. Wesley divides the fuel by rank, the thorns being the low and mean and the forest the tall trees standing thick with boughs entangled, readier to catch and spread the fire. Calvin uses the figure against those who blame God: the calamities are the fire, but the wickedness of men is the fuel by which the anger of God is kindled, so that men complain the wrath of God burns violently without considering that their own sins are the fans which inflame it. He finds a gradation in it: the Lord proceeds gently at first, doubles the punishment when light chastisement does no good, and if he sees us obstinate burns to the uttermost. Ellicott alone finds something beyond destruction here: for such a people sin becomes the punishment of sin and burns like fire in a thicket, leaving the land clear for fresh culture and a better growth.
19:
The darkening of the land is taken two ways. Gill reads it figuratively of great distress, connecting it with the smoke of the previous verse, since fire in the thickets fills the air with darkness; this sense of the word is met with only here, he notes, and is supported by three commentators from its use in Arabic, but two ancient versions and a paraphrase render it instead that the whole land is burned, which he thinks agrees with the context. Calvin keeps the darkness and makes it the strongest word available: the vengeance is described by that metaphor, than which nothing can be more dismal, for without figures a judgment so revolting cannot be expressed; and he too hears the fire behind it, since when a conflagration rages the light is overpowered by thick smoke. Having shown that the cause of all our evils proceeds from ourselves, he adds that God is still a most righteous avenger, not because he is inclined to cruelty but because he is just and cannot endure the wicked.

What follows is read as civil war. Calvin states the principle plainly: when no enemies are to be seen whom we have cause to dread, God will arm us against ourselves, ruining us by intestine broils. That every man should devour his own flesh is shocking to relate, and yet when the Lord has blinded us what remains but that we destroy each other; monstrous as it is, it happens almost every day. He presses it by comparison with the animals: we are restrained by no bond of blood or religion, nor by the image of God we all bear, though the heathen were kept from injuring each other by a common nature, seeing that a wolf does not devour a wolf, nor a bear a bear. Gill describes the snatching, either with the hand, plundering all within reach, or with the teeth like beasts of prey, rending whatever comes in the way. Calvin adds that the phrase denotes either insatiable covetousness or insatiable cruelty, and finds the bitterness heightened because it is the children of Abraham who break out into such beastly fury.

Clarke thinks the received text has gone wrong at the crucial word. Where it reads the flesh of his own arm he would read the flesh of his neighbour, reporting that one Greek manuscript carries a double version of which one half reads a word meaning neighbour, and that the Chaldee reads the same; a later prophet, he adds, has the very same expression. The context confirms it, he argues, since the next verse explains the general idea by instances: two tribes most closely connected in blood and situation destroy each other, and both, amid their own dissensions, agree in preying on a third. Gill reads that verse the same way, of quarrels and wars among themselves by which they consumed each other though they were brethren, and notes that several versions render the bare names as devouring. Wesley marks only the closeness of the pair, nearer and dearer to one another than any other tribe, being both sons of one father. Calvin traces the relationship further and turns it into the point of the threat: though descended from one ancestor and closely allied through one patriarch, they are made to destroy themselves by mutual conflict, so that there is no need of foreign enemies, and having wearied themselves with mutual wounds they unite against the remaining kingdom. He closes on the sequence of blows. Anyone considering the calamities already threatened will be astonished that severer chastisements follow; but this is how God acts towards the wicked, not ceasing to afflict those who, after being frequently invited, refuse to be reconciled. Rods are prepared, he says, that God may strike with them at once, for his anger is not a passion that spends itself but is immediately followed by revenge.
